content.title: About
content.content: Catfish fillet is the tender meat of a freshwater fish, obtained after removing bones and skin. When baked or broiled, the fillet has a soft texture, a mildly sweet flavor, and a moderate fat content, making it a popular choice for healthy eating.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Catfish belong to the Siluriformes order and are found in rivers and lakes across North America, Europe, and Asia.
The flesh is high in protein and contains few bones, simplifying preparation.
Catfish can breathe air using a specialized organ, allowing them to survive in low‑oxygen waters.
In cuisine, catfish is often prepared "à la française" – baked with herbs and lemon.
Because it is a "soft" fish, catfish is frequently recommended for children and people with digestive sensitivities.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: A 100‑g serving of catfish fillet provides about 18 g of high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many marine fish, catfish contains relatively little saturated fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Catfish supplies vitamin B12, niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which support nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Minerals: phosphorus and selenium
items.content: Phosphorus is important for bone health, while selenium acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Moderate omega‑3 content
items.content: Although lower than fatty ocean fish, catfish still contributes omega‑3 fatty acids that benefit cardiovascular health.

items.title: Heavy‑metal contamination
items.content: Like many freshwater species, catfish can accumulate cadmium and mercury in polluted waters; purchase from reputable sources.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Sodium content in prepared dishes
items.content: When seasoned with soy sauce or marinades, sodium levels can rise sharply, which is undesirable for hypertension.

items.title: Potential parasites
items.content: Raw or undercooked pieces may harbor parasites; always cook to an internal temperature of at least 63 °C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Catfish fillet can be baked in the oven with lemon, herbs, and olive oil, pan‑seared until golden, or steamed. It is often added to salads, soups, pasta, and rice dishes. Before cooking, rinse and pat dry the fillet, then season with salt and pepper if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh catfish fillet in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C, wrapped in plastic film or an airtight container, for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze in a sealed bag at –18 °C, where it retains quality for up to 3 months. Thaw frozen fillet in the refrigerator before cooking.
